newsitem.title: FRANCE: Interior minister Chevenement is anti-U.S. leftist.
newsitem.headline: Interior minister Chevenement is anti-U.S. leftist.

text.p: Jean-Pierre Chevenement, appointed French interior minister on Wednesday, is a militant leftist and nationalist best known for resigning as defence minister during the Gulf War because he disagreed with its aims.
He remains one of the most virulent left-wing campaigners against the Maastricht treaty on European union, arguing that the planned single European currency will subject France to rule by Germany.

But he will have to put up with Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's pro-European policy to keep his key cabinet post responsible for internal security, terrorism, the fight against drugs and illegal immigration and the network of prefects who represent the government across the country.

In a political establishment where many regard the United States as a rival, Chevenement is fiercely anti-American. That and sympathy for Iraqi President Saddam Hussein and for secular Arab nationalism led him to quit at the height of the Gulf War.

A member of the Franco-Iraqi parliamentary friendship group, he recently accused Washington of treating Iraq "not like a country with a population but like a petroleum reserve...The Iraqi people are being treated like Apache Indians at the end of the 19th century".
Aged 58, his power base is in Belfort in eastern France.

After long heading the left-wing CERES faction, he resigned from the Socialist party in 1992 in protest at its support for the Maastricht treaty, as well as what he called corruption and a drift to the right. He founded the Citizen's Movement (MDC), which won seven seats in Sunday's general election.
Chevenement helped the late Francois Mitterrand build the modern Socialist party in the 1970s, had long been a left-wing dissident on its fringes and has a history of resignations.
He was the only senior Socialist to campaign against the Maastricht treaty, saying it would create a capitalists' Europe of high unemployment.
On quitting the Socialist executive in July 1992, he said the party had become "tasteless, colourless and odourless".

His beliefs in a key role for the state in economic planning were reflected in the Socialist programme of the 1970s, and he was given the post of industry and research minister when Mitterrand was elected president in 1981.
Chevenement helped implement a wave of nationalisations but resigned in 1983 when Mitterrand shifted to a more pragmatic, orthodox economic policy.
In a typically blunt resignation statement, he said: "A minister either shuts his mouth or quits."

He returned as a respected education minister in 1984-86, reimposing traditional discipline in French schools, restoring civic instruction and criticising what he saw as laxity among left-wing teachers dominant since the May 1968 student unrest.

The military respected his keen knowledge of defence matters but were outraged when he insisted at the outset of the Gulf crisis that French combat planes not be posted on the same Saudi airfields as their American comrades.
Son of country schoolteachers, he studied at the Political Science Institute and Ecole Nationale d'Administration civil service college.
